name: dterm
description: Persistent terminal sessions per workspace with auto-reattach. Self-contained — no external daemon required.

dterm.autoReconnect.description: On workspace open, recreate VS Code terminals for each live daemon session that belongs to this workspace.

dterm.scrollbackLines.description: Daemon-side scrollback retention in lines, replayed on reattach. 0 follows `terminal.integrated.scrollback` (recommended). A positive value overrides; values greater than `terminal.integrated.scrollback` will be silently truncated by xterm.js on attach.

dterm.shell.description: Override the shell executable used for new sessions. Empty = $SHELL or /bin/bash.

dterm.shellArgs.description: Arguments passed to the shell on new sessions.

enumDescriptions: Use systemd-run --user only when it actually buys something: Linux, user-systemd accepts units, AND logind has KillUserProcesses=yes (the one case where the double-fork's reparent-to-init isn't enough). Otherwise falls back silently to double-fork.
Use systemd-run --user whenever user-systemd accepts units, even on systems where double-fork would also work. Gives you journalctl integration / systemctl --user visibility unconditionally.
Always use the legacy double-fork. Skips the systemd-run path and the linger prompt entirely.
dterm.useSystemdRun.markdownDescription:
Daemon spawn strategy on Linux. The systemd-run path runs the daemon as a transient `--user` service so it's reparented to user-systemd, visible via `systemctl --user list-units dterm-daemon`, and survives logind's `KillUserProcesses=yes`.

- `auto` (default): only used when there's a real benefit -- specifically when `KillUserProcesses=yes` would have killed the double-forked daemon at session end. On the much more common `KillUserProcesses=no` configurations, double-fork is already fully durable, so nothing changes.
- `always`: take the systemd-run path whenever user-systemd accepts units, even on `KillUserProcesses=no`. Useful if you want the `journalctl --user -u dterm-daemon` integration unconditionally.
- `never`: always use the legacy double-fork.

When the systemd-run path is selected, dterm checks whether lingering is enabled (`loginctl enable-linger`); if not, you'll be prompted to enable it before the first spawn. Without lingering the daemon would die on SSH disconnect, defeating the point of dterm.

dterm.instanceId.markdownDescription:
Namespace for the dterm daemon. When non-empty, dterm uses a separate daemon process, socket, log file, and session pool keyed by this id -- so the marketplace build and a locally-installed/sideloaded copy don't fight over the same sessions.

Leave empty for the default (recommended). The extension auto-detects VS Code's Extension Development Host (F5 debug) and uses `dev` automatically there; this setting overrides that auto-detection.

A window reload is required after changing this setting.

dterm.tabTitle.markdownDescription:
Tab-title template for dterm terminals. When non-empty, overrides `#terminal.integrated.tabs.title#` for dterm sessions only. Empty = inherit `#terminal.integrated.tabs.title#`.

Supports the standard VS Code variables (`${process}`, `${cwd}`, `${cwdFolder}`, `${workspaceFolder}`, `${workspaceFolderName}`, `${sequence}`, `${separator}`) plus two dterm-specific additions:

- `${session}` -- the underlying dterm session id (e.g. `vscode-myproject-1`). Stable for the lifetime of the session across reattach; useful for disambiguating multiple identically-named tabs or for debugging.
- `${workspace}` -- alias for `vscode.workspace.name`. Stable across multi-root workspaces (returns the `.code-workspace` file name or single-folder name) where `${workspaceFolder}` only ever points at the first folder.

Variables that don't apply to dterm Pseudoterminals (`${task}`, `${local}`, `${shellType}`, `${shellCommand}`, `${shellPromptInput}`, `${progress}`, `${fixedDimensions}`) resolve to empty, and the surrounding `${separator}` collapses accordingly.
